cards.q: How many neurons carry the signal from the central nervous system to the effector in a somatic motor pathway?
cards.a: One.
options: One
Two
Three
Four
cards.explanation: A single somatic motor neuron runs the whole way, from its cell body in the CNS out to the skeletal muscle fiber, with no synapse in between. Two is the autonomic arrangement, where a preganglionic and a postganglionic neuron are linked at a ganglion. Three and four do not describe any motor output pathway, although a sensory pathway climbing to the cortex does use three neurons in series.

cards.q: How many neurons in series make up an autonomic motor pathway from the central nervous system to the effector?
cards.a: Two.
options: One
Four
Two
Three
cards.explanation: Every autonomic pathway uses a preganglionic neuron whose cell body sits in the CNS and a postganglionic neuron whose cell body sits in a ganglion outside the CNS. One neuron is the somatic pattern that runs straight to skeletal muscle. Three and four overcount, since only one peripheral synapse exists between the CNS and the target organ.

cards.q: Where do the two neurons of an autonomic pathway synapse with each other?
cards.a: In an autonomic ganglion outside the central nervous system.
options: In the ventral horn of the spinal cord
In an autonomic ganglion outside the central nervous system
In the dorsal root ganglion
Within the wall of the effector cell itself
cards.explanation: The peripheral synapse happens in an autonomic ganglion, a cluster of postganglionic cell bodies sitting outside the CNS, which is exactly the relay the somatic system lacks. The ventral horn holds the cell bodies of preganglionic and somatic motor neurons, not the relay itself. The dorsal root ganglion holds sensory cell bodies and has no synapse in it at all, and no synapse occurs inside the effector cell.

cards.q: Which tissue is the only effector of the somatic motor system?
cards.a: Skeletal muscle.
options: Cardiac muscle
Smooth muscle
Glandular epithelium
Skeletal muscle
cards.explanation: Somatic motor neurons end on skeletal muscle fibers and on nothing else, which is why the division is often called the voluntary motor system. Cardiac muscle, smooth muscle, and glandular epithelium are the three autonomic effectors and receive no somatic innervation at all.

cards.q: Which set of tissues does the autonomic nervous system innervate?
cards.a: Cardiac muscle, smooth muscle, and glands.
options: Cardiac muscle, smooth muscle, and glands
Skeletal muscle and cardiac muscle only
Smooth muscle and skeletal muscle only
Glands and skeletal muscle only
cards.explanation: The autonomic output reaches cardiac muscle, smooth muscle everywhere in the body, and secretory glands, which is the full list of involuntary effectors. Every wrong option smuggles skeletal muscle into the autonomic list, and skeletal muscle is somatic territory. Skeletal muscle blood vessels are autonomic, but the vessel wall is smooth muscle, not the muscle fibers themselves.

cards.q: Where is the cell body of an autonomic preganglionic neuron located?
cards.a: In the brainstem or spinal cord.
options: In a paravertebral ganglion
In a ganglion near the target organ
In the brainstem or spinal cord
In the wall of the innervated organ
cards.explanation: The preganglionic cell body is inside the CNS, in a brainstem nucleus or the lateral horn of the spinal cord, and its axon leaves to find a ganglion. Paravertebral ganglia and ganglia near the target organ hold postganglionic cell bodies, which are the second neuron. Cell bodies in the organ wall belong to enteric neurons or terminal ganglia, again postganglionic.

cards.q: Which neurotransmitter does a somatic motor neuron release onto skeletal muscle, and at which receptor does it act?
cards.a: Acetylcholine at a nicotinic receptor.
options: Norepinephrine at a beta-1 receptor
Acetylcholine at a muscarinic receptor
Norepinephrine at an alpha-1 receptor
Acetylcholine at a nicotinic receptor
cards.explanation: The neuromuscular junction uses acetylcholine acting on nicotinic receptors, which are ligand gated cation channels that depolarize the muscle fiber quickly and reliably. Muscarinic receptors also bind acetylcholine but they sit on parasympathetic target organs, never on skeletal muscle. Norepinephrine at beta-1 or alpha-1 receptors is a sympathetic postganglionic arrangement and has no role at the neuromuscular junction.

cards.q: What effect can a somatic motor neuron have on the skeletal muscle fiber it innervates?
cards.a: Excitation only.
options: Excitation only
Inhibition only
Excitation or inhibition depending on the receptor
Neither, since it only sets resting tone
cards.explanation: Somatic motor neurons are always excitatory, so the only way to relax a skeletal muscle is to stop firing on it. Autonomic output is the branch that can either excite or inhibit, because the receptor on the target decides the response. Inhibition only is never true of a motor neuron, and setting resting tone without excitation misdescribes what the neuromuscular junction does.

cards.q: A fiber leaves the spinal cord, synapses on a second neuron in a ganglion, and that second neuron ends on a salivary gland. How is this pathway classified?
cards.a: Autonomic, because it uses two neurons and ends on a gland.
options: Somatic, because the fiber originates in the spinal cord
Autonomic, because it uses two neurons and ends on a gland
Somatic, because it includes a peripheral ganglion
Autonomic, because the first neuron is myelinated
cards.explanation: Two features settle it at once: a peripheral synapse in a ganglion and an effector that is a gland rather than skeletal muscle. Originating in the spinal cord does not distinguish the systems, since both preganglionic and somatic motor cell bodies live there. A peripheral ganglion is the opposite of a somatic feature, and myelination of the first neuron is true but is not the defining criterion asked for.

cards.q: A drug blocks nicotinic receptors only in autonomic ganglia and does not reach the neuromuscular junction. What happens to voluntary movement of the biceps?
cards.a: It is unaffected, because the somatic pathway has no ganglion.
options: It becomes weak, because the relay through the ganglion has been lost
It becomes uncoordinated, because resting tone in the muscle is lost
It is unaffected, because the somatic pathway has no ganglion
It stops entirely, because acetylcholine can no longer act anywhere
cards.explanation: The somatic motor neuron runs from the cord to the muscle with no intervening synapse, so a drug confined to ganglia has nothing to block in that pathway. Weakness from a lost relay assumes a ganglion that does not exist in the somatic route. Loss of tone and complete arrest both assume the drug reached the neuromuscular junction, which the question rules out.

cards.q: A toxin blocks acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction only. What happens to intestinal smooth muscle?
cards.a: It continues to contract normally.
options: It becomes flaccid along with skeletal muscle
It contracts continuously without relaxing
It loses all spontaneous activity
It continues to contract normally
cards.explanation: Intestinal smooth muscle is an autonomic effector, so a toxin restricted to the neuromuscular junction never touches it and gut motility carries on. Flaccidity along with skeletal muscle mistakes smooth muscle for a somatic target. Continuous contraction and loss of spontaneous activity both assume the toxin altered autonomic or enteric input, which it did not.

cards.q: A somatic motor nerve to a limb muscle is cut. What is the immediate consequence for that muscle?
cards.a: Complete flaccid paralysis, because it has no other motor input.
options: Complete flaccid paralysis, because it has no other motor input
Reduced but continuing contraction driven by the opposing autonomic division
Continuous contraction produced by unopposed excitatory input
Normal contraction maintained by pacemaker cells inside the muscle itself
cards.explanation: Skeletal muscle is innervated by one excitatory neuron and nothing else, so cutting that neuron leaves the fiber with no way to be activated. There is no opposing division for skeletal muscle, which is what makes it different from a dually innervated organ. Skeletal muscle fibers also have no pacemaker activity of their own, unlike cardiac and much smooth muscle.

cards.q: Which structure would you find in a pathway to the stomach but never in a pathway to the quadriceps?
cards.a: A peripheral ganglion containing a synapse.
options: A myelinated axon leaving the spinal cord
A peripheral ganglion containing a synapse
A terminal that releases acetylcholine
A neuronal cell body located inside the central nervous system
cards.explanation: The peripheral ganglion is the structural signature of the autonomic route, since the somatic neuron reaches its muscle without relaying anywhere. Myelinated axons leaving the cord, acetylcholine release, and CNS cell bodies all occur in both systems, so none of them can separate the two. Acetylcholine in particular is used by every preganglionic fiber and by every somatic motor neuron.

cards.q: Why does a signal leaving the spinal cord reach the heart with more synaptic delay than a signal leaving the cord reaches a leg muscle?
cards.a: The autonomic route includes an extra synapse at the ganglion.
options: Cardiac muscle responds more slowly to depolarization than skeletal muscle does
The autonomic route includes an extra synapse at the ganglion
The heart is a greater distance from the spinal cord than the muscles of the leg
Autonomic axons carry an action potential of smaller amplitude
cards.explanation: Each chemical synapse costs about half a millisecond, and the autonomic pathway pays that cost twice, once in the ganglion and once at the target, while the somatic pathway pays it once. Distance is not the explanation, and the heart is in fact closer to the thoracic cord than the foot is. Action potential size does not vary with the pathway, since action potentials are all or none, and the properties of the effector do not change the delay in the nerve.

cards.q: Autonomic input to an organ is removed surgically. Why does the organ usually keep working at some level while a denervated skeletal muscle does not?
cards.a: Cardiac and smooth muscle generate their own activity, while skeletal muscle cannot.
options: Autonomic axons regrow across the cut within a few minutes
The organ on the opposite side takes over the lost function
Cardiac and smooth muscle generate their own activity, while skeletal muscle cannot
Glands and smooth muscle are not truly innervated in the first place
cards.explanation: Autonomic effectors modulate an activity they already have, since pacemaker cells in the heart and gut fire on their own, so removing the nerve changes the rate rather than abolishing the function. Skeletal muscle has no intrinsic activity and is silent without its motor neuron. Axons do not regrow in minutes, no contralateral takeover exists for visceral organs, and glands are genuinely innervated.

cards.q: A toxin prevents acetylcholine release from every cholinergic terminal in the body. Predict the effect on skeletal muscle contraction and on transmission through autonomic ganglia.
cards.a: Skeletal muscle is paralyzed and ganglionic transmission fails in both autonomic divisions.
options: Skeletal muscle is paralyzed and ganglionic transmission fails in both autonomic divisions
Skeletal muscle is paralyzed but transmission through both sets of autonomic ganglia continues normally
Skeletal muscle is spared but ganglionic transmission fails
Only parasympathetic ganglia fail, since sympathetic ganglia use norepinephrine
cards.explanation: Acetylcholine is the transmitter at the neuromuscular junction and at every autonomic ganglion, sympathetic and parasympathetic alike, so blocking its release takes out both. Sparing the ganglia forgets that all preganglionic fibers are cholinergic. Sparing skeletal muscle forgets the neuromuscular junction, and the claim that sympathetic ganglia run on norepinephrine confuses the preganglionic transmitter with the postganglionic one, since norepinephrine is released at the sympathetic target rather than in the ganglion.

cards.q: A researcher traces a nerve to the bladder and finds the first cell body in the sacral spinal cord, a synapse in a ganglion in the bladder wall, and a short second fiber ending on smooth muscle. Which conclusion is supported?
cards.a: This is an autonomic pathway, since it has two neurons and a smooth muscle effector.
options: This is a somatic motor pathway, since the first cell body sits inside the spinal cord
This is a sensory pathway, since the ganglion lies outside the central nervous system
This is an autonomic pathway, since it has two neurons and a smooth muscle effector
This is a somatic pathway, since the second fiber is short
cards.explanation: Two neurons in series, a peripheral ganglion, and smooth muscle as the target are together decisive for an autonomic motor pathway. A spinal cord cell body is common to both motor systems and proves nothing on its own. A peripheral ganglion is also present in sensory pathways, but a dorsal root ganglion contains no synapse and does not end on smooth muscle, and the length of the second fiber is a divisional clue rather than a somatic one.

cards.q: After a complete spinal cord transection at T6, a patient has no voluntary leg movement, yet the heart continues to beat and the intestines still move contents along. What best explains the difference between the two effectors?
cards.a: Skeletal muscle depends entirely on descending somatic drive, while cardiac and smooth muscle have intrinsic pacemaker activity that autonomic nerves only modulate.
options: The heart and gut are innervated by somatic motor nerves that were spared below the level of the injury, while the leg nerves were not
The legs receive dual autonomic innervation, and the transection interrupted both of those inputs at the same time
Skeletal muscle depends entirely on descending somatic drive, while cardiac and smooth muscle have intrinsic pacemaker activity that autonomic nerves only modulate
Autonomic axons conduct faster than somatic axons and can carry their signals across the damaged segment of the cord
cards.explanation: The heart and gut set their own baseline rhythm, so losing part of their autonomic input alters how fast they work rather than whether they work, while a skeletal muscle with no command from above simply does not contract. The heart and gut have no somatic innervation to spare. Skeletal muscle is never dually innervated, and autonomic axons are in fact slower, being thinly myelinated or unmyelinated, and no axon crosses a complete transection.

cards.q: Two nerves are recorded during a reflex. Nerve A shows one action potential from cord to effector with a single synaptic delay at the end. Nerve B shows a delay partway along the route and a second delay at the effector. Which effectors are the most likely targets of A and B?
cards.a: A ends on skeletal muscle and B ends on a gland.
options: A ends on cardiac muscle and B ends on skeletal muscle
A ends on a gland and B ends on skeletal muscle
A ends on smooth muscle and B ends on cardiac muscle
A ends on skeletal muscle and B ends on a gland
cards.explanation: A single terminal delay marks a one neuron somatic route, whose only possible target is skeletal muscle, while a mid route delay marks the ganglionic synapse of a two neuron autonomic route, whose targets are cardiac muscle, smooth muscle, and glands. The options that put cardiac or smooth muscle on the single delay route forget that no visceral effector is reached without a ganglion. The option placing skeletal muscle on the two delay route makes the same error in reverse.

cards.q: From which spinal segments do sympathetic preganglionic fibers leave the central nervous system?
cards.a: T1 through L2.
options: T1 through L2
C1 through C8
S2 through S4
L3 through S1
cards.explanation: Sympathetic preganglionic cell bodies sit in the lateral horn from the first thoracic through the second lumbar segment, which is why the division is called thoracolumbar. S2 through S4 is the sacral half of the parasympathetic outflow. The cervical and lower lumbar segments contain no autonomic preganglionic cell bodies, although sympathetic fibers do travel up the chain to reach the head.

cards.q: Where does parasympathetic output leave the central nervous system?
cards.a: From the brainstem by cranial nerves and from spinal segments S2 to S4.
options: From the thoracic and upper lumbar segments of the spinal cord only
From the brainstem by cranial nerves and from spinal segments S2 to S4
From the cervical segments of the spinal cord and from the brainstem
From every spinal segment along the whole length of the cord
cards.explanation: The parasympathetic division is craniosacral, leaving in cranial nerves III, VII, IX, and X and in the sacral roots from S2 to S4. Thoracic and lumbar outflow is the sympathetic pattern. The cervical cord carries no preganglionic cell bodies of either division, and no division leaves at every level.

cards.q: Where are most sympathetic ganglia located?
cards.a: In a chain alongside the vertebral column, close to the spinal cord.
options: Inside the wall of each individual target organ
Within the brainstem, next to the nuclei of the cranial nerves
In a chain alongside the vertebral column, close to the spinal cord
Scattered through the mesentery, just outside the wall of each organ
cards.explanation: Sympathetic ganglia lie in the paravertebral chain flanking the vertebral column, with a few prevertebral ganglia in front of the aorta, so the relay happens near the cord rather than near the target. Ganglia inside the organ wall are the parasympathetic pattern. Ganglia are by definition outside the CNS, so the brainstem option cannot be right.

cards.q: Where are parasympathetic ganglia located?
cards.a: In or very near the wall of the target organ.
options: In a chain beside the vertebral column
In the lateral horn of the spinal cord
In front of the abdominal aorta
In or very near the wall of the target organ
cards.explanation: Parasympathetic ganglia sit on or in the organ they supply, which is why the postganglionic fiber is so short. The paravertebral chain and the prevertebral ganglia in front of the aorta are both sympathetic locations. The lateral horn is inside the spinal cord and holds preganglionic cell bodies, not a ganglion.

cards.q: In the sympathetic division, how do the lengths of the preganglionic and postganglionic fibers compare?
cards.a: The preganglionic fiber is short and the postganglionic fiber is long.
options: The preganglionic fiber is short and the postganglionic fiber is long
The preganglionic fiber is long and the postganglionic fiber is short
Both fibers are about the same length
Both fibers are short, since the ganglion sits midway
cards.explanation: Because the sympathetic ganglion is near the cord, the first fiber has only a short distance to travel and the second must cover the rest of the way to the organ. The long preganglionic and short postganglionic pattern is parasympathetic, and it follows directly from where that division puts its ganglia. Equal lengths would require a ganglion halfway to every organ, which neither division uses.

cards.q: Which nerve carries most of the parasympathetic supply to the thoracic and abdominal organs?
cards.a: The vagus nerve.
options: The phrenic nerve
The vagus nerve
The greater splanchnic nerve
The pelvic splanchnic nerve
cards.explanation: The vagus, cranial nerve X, supplies the heart, lungs, stomach, and most of the intestine, carrying the great majority of parasympathetic traffic below the neck. The greater splanchnic nerve is sympathetic preganglionic fiber heading for prevertebral ganglia. The pelvic splanchnic nerves are parasympathetic but serve only the distal colon and pelvic organs, and the phrenic nerve is somatic motor to the diaphragm.

cards.q: What is the effect of parasympathetic activity on heart rate?
cards.a: It slows heart rate.
options: It raises heart rate
It slows heart rate
It leaves heart rate unchanged but raises contractility
It raises heart rate only during inspiration
cards.explanation: Vagal activity slows depolarization of the sinoatrial node, so the firing rate and therefore the heart rate falls. Raising heart rate is the sympathetic effect. The parasympathetic division has little influence on ventricular contractility, so holding rate steady while raising contractility reverses the true pattern, and the inspiratory rise in rate is caused by reduced vagal activity rather than increased vagal activity.

cards.q: What is the effect of sympathetic activity on gastrointestinal motility and secretion?
cards.a: Both decrease.
options: Motility increases and secretion decreases
Both increase
Both decrease
Motility decreases and secretion increases
cards.explanation: Sympathetic output turns digestion down as a unit, slowing smooth muscle in the gut wall and reducing glandular secretion while blood is directed elsewhere. Increases in both are the parasympathetic pattern of rest and digest. The two split options describe a mismatch that does not occur, since the division acts on motility and secretion in the same direction.

cards.q: A student begins to sprint and sympathetic output to the heart rises sharply. Predict the change in heart rate.
cards.a: Heart rate rises.
options: Heart rate falls
Heart rate rises
Heart rate is unchanged while stroke volume falls
Heart rate rises only after the sprint ends
cards.explanation: Sympathetic fibers to the sinoatrial node speed its pacemaker depolarization, so more sympathetic traffic means a faster rate, and the change begins within a few beats. A fall in rate would require increased vagal activity instead. Stroke volume rises rather than falls under sympathetic drive, and the response happens during the effort, not after it.

cards.q: After a large meal, parasympathetic outflow to the gut increases. Predict what happens to intestinal motility and glandular secretion.
cards.a: Both increase.
options: Both decrease
Motility increases while secretion falls
Both increase
Motility falls while secretion rises
cards.explanation: Parasympathetic activity is the digestive setting, raising smooth muscle activity in the gut wall and stimulating secretion so food is moved and broken down. Decreases in both would follow sympathetic activation instead. The mixed options split two responses that this division always drives in the same direction.

cards.q: In an anesthetized animal the vagus nerve is stimulated electrically. Predict the effect on the sinoatrial node.
cards.a: It depolarizes more slowly, so the heart rate falls.
options: It depolarizes more slowly, so the heart rate falls
It depolarizes faster, so the heart rate rises
It stops responding to any input at all
It is unaffected, since the vagus supplies only the lungs
cards.explanation: Vagal stimulation releases acetylcholine on the sinoatrial node, slowing its pacemaker drift toward threshold and lowering the rate. Faster depolarization is what sympathetic stimulation produces. The node keeps responding to other inputs during vagal stimulation, and the vagus supplies the heart as well as the lungs and abdominal viscera.

cards.q: A lesion destroys the lateral horn neurons from T1 to L2 while leaving the brainstem and sacral cord intact. Which division is lost?
cards.a: The sympathetic division.
options: The parasympathetic division
Both divisions equally
The sympathetic division
Neither, since these neurons are somatic
cards.explanation: T1 to L2 is exactly the thoracolumbar outflow, so destroying those lateral horn cell bodies removes the sympathetic preganglionic supply. The parasympathetic division survives because its cell bodies are craniosacral and the lesion spares both the brainstem and S2 to S4. Lateral horn neurons are autonomic preganglionic, not somatic, which is why voluntary movement would be relatively preserved.

cards.q: A dissection shows a very long preganglionic fiber that finally synapses in a small ganglion sitting on the wall of the bladder. Which division is this?
cards.a: Parasympathetic, because the ganglion is at the target organ.
options: Sympathetic, because the first fiber travels a long distance
Parasympathetic, because the ganglion is at the target organ
Sympathetic, because the bladder sits among the pelvic organs
Parasympathetic, because every long autonomic fiber is cholinergic
cards.explanation: Ganglion position is the reliable clue: a relay in the organ wall means a parasympathetic pathway, and the long first fiber follows from that geometry. A long fiber alone does not identify a division, since sympathetic postganglionic fibers are long too. The bladder receives both divisions, so its location settles nothing, and being cholinergic does not track fiber length, since every preganglionic fiber in both divisions releases acetylcholine.

cards.q: Why does a burst of sympathetic activity usually affect many organs at once while a burst of parasympathetic activity is more targeted?
cards.a: Each sympathetic preganglionic fiber diverges onto many postganglionic neurons in the chain.
options: Sympathetic axons conduct much faster than parasympathetic axons do, so more organs respond
Parasympathetic fibers release a weaker neurotransmitter with a smaller effect on the target
Each sympathetic preganglionic fiber diverges onto many postganglionic neurons in the chain
Sympathetic ganglia contain no synapses at all, so incoming signals pass straight through them
cards.explanation: A single sympathetic preganglionic fiber can synapse on dozens of postganglionic neurons spread up and down the paravertebral chain, so one input fans out to many targets, while a parasympathetic fiber ends in a ganglion serving one organ. Conduction speed does not determine how many organs respond. Acetylcholine is not a weaker transmitter, and sympathetic ganglia certainly contain synapses, which is where the divergence happens.

cards.q: A person is startled by a loud noise. Predict the simultaneous change in heart rate and in gastrointestinal motility.
cards.a: Heart rate rises and gastrointestinal motility falls.
options: Heart rate falls and gastrointestinal motility rises
Both heart rate and gastrointestinal motility rise
Both heart rate and gastrointestinal motility fall
Heart rate rises and gastrointestinal motility falls
cards.explanation: A startle recruits the sympathetic division, which speeds the sinoatrial node while inhibiting gut smooth muscle, shifting resources from digestion to circulation. Falling rate with rising motility is the parasympathetic pattern seen after a meal. The two options that move both variables the same way miss the point that this division pushes the heart and the gut in opposite directions.

cards.q: A drug blocks synaptic transmission only in ganglia located within organ walls and does not reach the paravertebral chain. Predict the effect on resting heart rate and on gastric motility.
cards.a: Heart rate rises and gastric motility falls.
options: Heart rate rises and gastric motility falls
Heart rate falls and gastric motility rises
Both are unchanged, since the chain is intact
Heart rate falls and gastric motility is unchanged
cards.explanation: Ganglia in organ walls are parasympathetic, so the drug removes vagal influence while leaving sympathetic transmission through the chain untouched. Losing the brake on the sinoatrial node lets the rate climb, and losing the parasympathetic drive to the stomach lowers motility. A slower heart with a more active stomach would describe losing sympathetic input instead. Nothing is unchanged, because the intact chain is now unopposed.

cards.q: Both vagus nerves are cut in an experimental animal. Predict the resting heart rate and the gastric secretion rate compared with before the cut.
cards.a: Heart rate is higher and gastric secretion is lower.
options: Heart rate is lower and gastric secretion is higher
Heart rate is higher and gastric secretion is higher
Heart rate is higher and gastric secretion is lower
Both are unchanged, since sympathetic input compensates
cards.explanation: The vagus carries parasympathetic fibers to both organs, so cutting it removes a slowing influence at the heart and a stimulating influence at the stomach, and the two effects therefore go in opposite directions. A lower rate would follow from losing sympathetic rather than vagal input. Higher secretion contradicts the loss of the main stimulus to gastric glands, and no compensation restores a signal the stomach no longer receives.

cards.q: A patient has a lesion confined to spinal segments S2 to S4. Which organ is most likely to show impaired autonomic control, and why is the heart spared?
cards.a: The distal colon is impaired, and the heart is spared because its parasympathetic supply is vagal.
options: The stomach is impaired, and the heart is spared because it receives sympathetic fibers only
The distal colon is impaired, and the heart is spared because its parasympathetic supply is vagal
The heart is impaired as well, since every parasympathetic fiber in the body leaves at sacral levels
The bronchi are impaired, and the heart is spared because it contains no autonomic ganglia
cards.explanation: Sacral preganglionic fibers in the pelvic splanchnic nerves supply the distal colon and pelvic organs, while the heart, stomach, and bronchi get their parasympathetic supply from the vagus, which leaves the brainstem well above the lesion. The stomach and bronchi are therefore spared for the same reason the heart is. The heart is not sympathetic only, since vagal fibers reach the sinoatrial node, and parasympathetic outflow is craniosacral rather than purely sacral.

cards.q: During a frightening event, preganglionic fibers from the upper thoracic cord fire into the paravertebral chain. Trace the consequence for the heart and explain why the effect outlasts the moment of fright.
cards.a: Postganglionic fibers speed the sinoatrial node, and circulating catecholamines from the adrenal medulla prolong the effect.
options: Postganglionic fibers slow the sinoatrial node, and a vagal rebound afterward prolongs that slowing for minutes
Postganglionic fibers speed the sinoatrial node, and circulating catecholamines from the adrenal medulla prolong the effect
Preganglionic fibers reach the sinoatrial node directly, so the whole effect ends the moment the firing stops
The chain relays into the vagus nerve, which then speeds the sinoatrial node for several minutes afterward
cards.explanation: Thoracic preganglionic fibers synapse in the chain, postganglionic fibers release norepinephrine on the sinoatrial node and raise the rate, and the same preganglionic outflow drives the adrenal medulla to release catecholamines into the blood, which are cleared slowly and keep the rate up after the alarm passes. Slowing the node is the vagal response. No preganglionic fiber reaches the heart directly, and the sympathetic chain does not relay into the vagus, which is a separate cranial nerve carrying the opposing division.

cards.q: Which neurotransmitter binds to nicotinic receptors?
cards.a: Acetylcholine.
options: Acetylcholine
Norepinephrine
Epinephrine
Dopamine
cards.explanation: Nicotinic receptors are cholinergic, so acetylcholine is their ligand, and the name comes from nicotine mimicking acetylcholine at this site. Norepinephrine and epinephrine bind adrenergic receptors, the alpha and beta family. Dopamine has its own receptors and is not the transmitter at ganglia or at the neuromuscular junction.

cards.q: Where are nicotinic receptors found in the autonomic nervous system?
cards.a: On the postganglionic neurons of every autonomic ganglion, sympathetic and parasympathetic.
options: On sympathetic ganglion neurons only
On parasympathetic ganglion neurons only
On the postganglionic neurons of every autonomic ganglion, sympathetic and parasympathetic
On the smooth muscle and gland cells at the end of every autonomic pathway, in both divisions
cards.explanation: Both divisions use acetylcholine at nicotinic receptors for the ganglionic synapse, which is the one step the two divisions share, and the same receptor appears at the skeletal neuromuscular junction. Restricting nicotinic receptors to one division misses that shared step. Target organ smooth muscle carries muscarinic or adrenergic receptors instead, so the nicotinic receptor is a relay receptor rather than an effector receptor.

cards.q: Which receptor does acetylcholine act on at a parasympathetic target organ?
cards.a: A muscarinic receptor.
options: A nicotinic receptor
A muscarinic receptor
A beta-1 receptor
An alpha-1 receptor
cards.explanation: Parasympathetic postganglionic fibers release acetylcholine onto muscarinic receptors on cardiac muscle, smooth muscle, and glands. Nicotinic receptors do bind acetylcholine, but in the autonomic system they sit in the ganglion, one synapse earlier. Beta-1 and alpha-1 are adrenergic and bind norepinephrine, so they belong to sympathetic targets.

cards.q: Which neurotransmitter do sympathetic postganglionic fibers release onto alpha and beta receptors?
cards.a: Norepinephrine.
options: Acetylcholine
Serotonin
Glutamate
Norepinephrine
cards.explanation: Sympathetic postganglionic terminals are adrenergic and release norepinephrine, which binds alpha and beta receptors on the target tissue. Acetylcholine is the transmitter one step earlier, in the ganglion, and also at parasympathetic targets. Serotonin and glutamate are central nervous system transmitters and are not used at autonomic effectors.

cards.q: Which adrenergic receptor subtype is the dominant one on cardiac muscle?
cards.a: Beta-1.
options: Alpha-1
Beta-1
Beta-2
Alpha-2
cards.explanation: Beta-1 receptors dominate on the sinoatrial node and the ventricular myocardium, so norepinephrine there raises rate and force of contraction. Beta-2 receptors are the ones on bronchiolar smooth muscle and on the vascular smooth muscle of skeletal muscle. Alpha-1 receptors are on most vascular smooth muscle, and alpha-2 receptors act mainly as presynaptic autoreceptors.

cards.q: Which receptor on bronchiolar smooth muscle produces relaxation when it is activated?
cards.a: Beta-2.
options: Alpha-1
Muscarinic
Beta-2
Nicotinic
cards.explanation: Beta-2 receptors on airway smooth muscle relax the bronchioles and widen the airway, which is why circulating epinephrine eases breathing. Muscarinic receptors are also on airway smooth muscle but do the opposite, constricting the bronchioles. Alpha-1 receptors are found on most vascular smooth muscle rather than on airways, and nicotinic receptors are on ganglion neurons and skeletal muscle, not on smooth muscle.

cards.q: Which receptor on most vascular smooth muscle produces vasoconstriction?
cards.a: Alpha-1.
options: Beta-1
Beta-2
Muscarinic
Alpha-1
cards.explanation: Alpha-1 receptors dominate on the smooth muscle of most arterioles, so norepinephrine narrows them and raises resistance. Beta-2 receptors on the vessels of skeletal muscle produce the opposite response, dilation, which is why blood is redistributed toward working muscle. Beta-1 receptors are the cardiac subtype, and vascular smooth muscle in general receives no parasympathetic muscarinic innervation.

cards.q: How does a nicotinic receptor produce its effect on the cell?
cards.a: It is a ligand gated ion channel that opens and lets cations enter.
options: It is a ligand gated ion channel that opens and lets cations enter
It is a G protein coupled receptor that changes cyclic AMP
It is an enzyme linked receptor that phosphorylates a target protein
It enters the cell and binds DNA to change transcription
cards.explanation: The nicotinic receptor is the channel itself, so binding acetylcholine opens a pore, cations flow in, and the cell depolarizes within milliseconds. Muscarinic and adrenergic receptors are the G protein coupled ones, which act through second messengers and are therefore slower. Enzyme linked receptors and intracellular DNA binding receptors belong to hormones such as insulin and cortisol, not to fast synaptic transmission.

cards.q: Acetylcholine is released onto muscarinic receptors on the sinoatrial node. Predict the change in heart rate.
cards.a: Heart rate falls.
options: Heart rate rises
Heart rate falls
Heart rate is unchanged but contractility rises
Heart rate rises and then falls below baseline
cards.explanation: Muscarinic activation on the node slows its pacemaker depolarization, so threshold is reached less often and the rate drops. A rise in rate would require beta-1 activation by norepinephrine instead. Contractility is a beta-1 effect on the ventricles, and there is no biphasic rise before the fall.

cards.q: Norepinephrine binds beta-1 receptors in the heart. Predict the effect on rate and on force of contraction.
cards.a: Both rate and force increase.
options: Rate increases and force decreases
Both rate and force decrease
Both rate and force increase
Rate is unchanged and force increases
cards.explanation: Beta-1 activation raises cyclic AMP in cardiac cells, which speeds the pacemaker current in the node and increases calcium entry in working myocardium, so the heart beats both faster and harder. Falling rate and force would follow muscarinic activation. Rate and force move together under beta-1 stimulation, so the split options describe a dissociation that does not occur here.

cards.q: Epinephrine activates beta-2 receptors on the arterioles supplying skeletal muscle. Predict the change in vessel diameter and in flow to that muscle.
cards.a: The vessels dilate and flow increases.
options: The vessels dilate and flow increases
The vessels constrict and flow decreases
The vessels constrict and flow increases
Diameter is unchanged and flow falls
cards.explanation: Beta-2 receptors relax vascular smooth muscle in skeletal muscle beds, so the arterioles widen, resistance falls, and more blood reaches the working muscle. Constriction is what alpha-1 activation would do, and alpha-1 is the dominant receptor in most other vascular beds. Constriction with increased flow is internally contradictory, since narrowing a vessel raises resistance and lowers flow at a given pressure.

cards.q: Norepinephrine reaches alpha-1 receptors on arterioles in the skin. Predict the change in vessel radius and in resistance in that bed.
cards.a: Radius falls and resistance rises.
options: Radius rises and resistance falls
Radius falls and resistance falls
Radius rises and resistance rises
Radius falls and resistance rises
cards.explanation: Alpha-1 activation contracts vascular smooth muscle, narrowing the arteriole, and resistance climbs steeply as radius falls. Widening with falling resistance is the beta-2 response, which occurs in skeletal muscle vessels rather than skin. The two mismatched options break the inverse relationship between radius and resistance that holds in every vascular bed.

cards.q: Acetylcholine acts on muscarinic receptors on bronchiolar smooth muscle. Predict the effect on airway diameter.
cards.a: The airway narrows.
options: The airway widens
The airway narrows
Diameter does not change, since airways lack muscarinic receptors
The airway widens only during expiration
cards.explanation: Muscarinic activation contracts airway smooth muscle, so the bronchioles narrow and resistance to airflow rises, which is the parasympathetic setting for the lungs. Widening is the beta-2 response to epinephrine on the same muscle, and holding those two opposite responses apart is the point of this pair. Airways do carry muscarinic receptors, and the response does not depend on the phase of breathing.

cards.q: A receptor on a postganglionic neuron responds to acetylcholine within a few milliseconds by opening a cation channel. Which receptor is it?
cards.a: A nicotinic receptor.
options: A muscarinic receptor
A beta-2 receptor
A nicotinic receptor
An alpha-1 receptor
cards.explanation: Speed plus a directly gated cation channel identifies the nicotinic receptor, which is why ganglionic transmission is fast and reliable. Muscarinic receptors also bind acetylcholine but work through G proteins, so their responses take longer and can be inhibitory. Beta-2 and alpha-1 receptors bind norepinephrine rather than acetylcholine and are also G protein coupled.

cards.q: A cell responds to norepinephrine with contraction of its smooth muscle. The response is blocked by an agent selective for alpha-1 receptors. Where is this cell most likely located?
cards.a: In the wall of an arteriole.
options: In the sinoatrial node
In the wall of an arteriole
In a bronchiole
In an autonomic ganglion
cards.explanation: Alpha-1 receptors driving contraction of smooth muscle is the signature of most vascular beds, where norepinephrine causes vasoconstriction. The sinoatrial node responds to norepinephrine through beta-1 receptors, and it is cardiac muscle rather than smooth muscle. Bronchiolar smooth muscle is dominated by beta-2 receptors that relax it, and ganglion neurons carry nicotinic receptors and are not muscle at all.

cards.q: An agent activates nicotinic receptors everywhere they occur. Predict what happens at autonomic ganglia and at skeletal muscle.
cards.a: Both sympathetic and parasympathetic ganglia are stimulated, and skeletal muscle is depolarized.
options: Only the sympathetic ganglia are driven, and skeletal muscle is left completely unaffected
Both sympathetic and parasympathetic ganglia are stimulated, and skeletal muscle is depolarized
Only the parasympathetic ganglia are driven, and skeletal muscle relaxes instead of contracting
Both sets of ganglia are unaffected, while skeletal muscle is strongly depolarized throughout the body
cards.explanation: Nicotinic receptors sit at every autonomic ganglion in both divisions and at the neuromuscular junction, so a nonselective activator drives all three sites at once and the visceral result is a confusing mixture of sympathetic and parasympathetic signs. Limiting the effect to one division ignores that both use the same ganglionic receptor. Sparing the ganglia or the muscle each ignores one of the two locations where this receptor is found.

cards.q: Circulating epinephrine reaches both the skin, where alpha-1 receptors dominate, and skeletal muscle vessels, where beta-2 receptors dominate. Predict how blood flow is distributed between the two beds.
cards.a: Skin flow falls and skeletal muscle flow rises.
options: Both beds receive more flow, since epinephrine dilates all vessels
Skin flow rises and skeletal muscle flow falls
Both beds receive less flow, since epinephrine constricts all vessels
Skin flow falls and skeletal muscle flow rises
cards.explanation: The same hormone produces opposite responses because the receptor on the tissue decides the outcome, so alpha-1 constriction in skin and beta-2 dilation in muscle together shunt blood toward the muscle that needs it. Treating epinephrine as a universal dilator or a universal constrictor misses that its effect is receptor dependent. Reversing the two beds inverts which receptor sits where.

cards.q: A substance raises heart rate and relaxes bronchiolar smooth muscle but produces no constriction of skin arterioles. Which receptor family is it acting on?
cards.a: Beta receptors.
options: Beta receptors
Alpha receptors
Muscarinic receptors
Nicotinic receptors
cards.explanation: Working back from the results, a faster heart points to beta-1 and relaxed airways to beta-2, while the absence of skin vasoconstriction rules out alpha-1 activity, so the agent is beta selective. Alpha activation would have constricted the skin vessels. Muscarinic activation would have slowed the heart and narrowed the airways, the reverse of both findings, and nicotinic activation would have driven both divisions at the ganglia rather than producing this clean pattern.

cards.q: Parasympathetic terminals release acetylcholine onto both the sinoatrial node and intestinal smooth muscle, yet the node slows while the intestine becomes more active. What accounts for the opposite outcomes?
cards.a: The two tissues carry different muscarinic receptor subtypes coupled to different intracellular pathways.
options: The intestine receives its acetylcholine from sympathetic rather than parasympathetic fibers
The two tissues carry different muscarinic receptor subtypes coupled to different intracellular pathways
Acetylcholine is broken down much faster at the sinoatrial node than it is in the intestinal wall
The sinoatrial node receives nicotinic input while the intestine receives muscarinic input instead
cards.explanation: The transmitter does not carry the instruction, the receptor does, and the muscarinic subtypes on cardiac and intestinal tissue couple to different G protein pathways, one that slows pacemaker depolarization and one that promotes contraction. Speed of breakdown changes how long a response lasts, not its direction. Sympathetic fibers to the gut release norepinephrine, and the sinoatrial node is not a ganglion, so it carries muscarinic rather than nicotinic receptors.

cards.q: What does it mean to say an organ is dually innervated?
cards.a: It receives input from both the sympathetic and the parasympathetic division.
options: It receives input from both the sympathetic and the parasympathetic division
It receives input from somatic motor neurons as well as autonomic neurons
It receives two separate preganglionic fibers that converge on a single ganglion
It is supplied by nerves arising from both the left and the right side of the cord
cards.explanation: Dual innervation means both autonomic divisions reach the same target, which usually lets the organ be pushed in either direction. Somatic plus autonomic input does not occur on the same effector, since skeletal muscle is somatic only. Convergence in a ganglion and bilateral supply are real features of nerve anatomy but neither one is what the term describes.

cards.q: What is autonomic tone?
cards.a: The steady background firing rate a division maintains at rest.
options: The maximum firing rate a division is able to reach
The steady background firing rate a division maintains at rest
The stiffness a muscle develops when it is stretched continuously
The delay between a stimulus arriving and the organ responding to it
cards.explanation: Autonomic fibers fire continuously at a low baseline rate, so the nervous system can raise or lower an organ activity simply by changing that ongoing rate. The maximum firing rate describes a ceiling, not the resting baseline. Stiffness from stretch is muscle tone in a mechanical sense, a different use of the word, and the delay to a response is latency.

cards.q: Which division exerts the greater tone on the heart in a resting person?
cards.a: The parasympathetic division.
options: The sympathetic division
Neither, since tone is absent at rest
The parasympathetic division
Both equally, so the rate sits at the intrinsic value
cards.explanation: Vagal tone dominates at rest, which is why the resting heart rate sits well below the pace the sinoatrial node would set on its own. Sympathetic tone to the heart is present but weaker at rest and rises with activity. Tone is not absent at rest, and if the two were balanced the rate would sit near the intrinsic value of about 100 beats per minute rather than near 70.

cards.q: What rate does the sinoatrial node set when all autonomic input to it is removed?
cards.a: About 100 beats per minute.
options: About 40 beats per minute
About 70 beats per minute
About 140 beats per minute
About 100 beats per minute
cards.explanation: Stripped of both divisions, the sinoatrial node depolarizes on its own at roughly 100 beats per minute, and that intrinsic rate is the reference point for judging tone. About 70 is the usual resting rate, which is lower precisely because vagal tone is holding the node back. About 40 is closer to what a ventricular pacemaker would produce, and 140 is a rate reached only with strong sympathetic drive.

cards.q: Which division maintains the resting tone of most arterioles?
cards.a: The sympathetic division.
options: The sympathetic division
The parasympathetic division
Both divisions in balance
Neither, since arteriolar diameter is set only locally
cards.explanation: Most arterioles receive sympathetic fibers only, and their continuous low level firing holds the vessels partly constricted, a baseline called vasomotor tone. The parasympathetic division does not supply the great majority of blood vessels, so a balance between divisions is not available there. Local metabolic factors also influence diameter, but they act on top of that sympathetic baseline rather than replacing it.

cards.q: Which of these structures receives sympathetic innervation only?
cards.a: Sweat glands of the skin.
options: The stomach
Sweat glands of the skin
The sinoatrial node
The bronchioles
cards.explanation: Sweat glands, piloerector muscles, most blood vessels, and the adrenal medulla are supplied by the sympathetic division alone, so they cannot be controlled by opposing inputs. The stomach, the sinoatrial node, and the bronchioles are all dually innervated and receive vagal fibers as well. Recognizing which targets are singly innervated tells you which ones must be regulated by changing one firing rate up and down.

cards.q: In a vessel supplied only by sympathetic fibers, how is vasodilation produced?
cards.a: By decreasing the sympathetic firing rate below its resting tone.
options: By recruiting parasympathetic fibers that also supply the vessel
By switching which transmitter is released from that same sympathetic fiber
By decreasing the sympathetic firing rate below its resting tone
By blocking the local metabolic signals that keep the vessel constricted
cards.explanation: Because the baseline is a partly constricted vessel, simply firing less allows the smooth muscle to relax, so one division achieves two directions by moving above and below its tone. There are no parasympathetic fibers to recruit in these beds. Neurons do not switch their transmitter from moment to moment, and local metabolites such as carbon dioxide dilate rather than constrict these vessels.

cards.q: In most dually innervated organs, how do the effects of the two divisions relate to each other?
cards.a: They are antagonistic, pushing the organ in opposite directions.
options: They are identical, so the effects add together
They are unrelated, since each targets a different tissue layer
They alternate, so only one division is active at a time
They are antagonistic, pushing the organ in opposite directions
cards.explanation: The usual arrangement is opposition, as at the heart where one division speeds the node and the other slows it, which gives fine control from two continuously active inputs. Identical effects occur in a few places such as the salivary glands, but that is the exception rather than the rule. Both divisions reach the same effector cells, and both are active at once rather than taking turns.

cards.q: A resting person has a heart rate of 72 beats per minute while the intrinsic rate of the sinoatrial node is about 100. What does this difference indicate?
cards.a: Parasympathetic tone is holding the rate down.
options: Sympathetic tone is holding the rate down
Parasympathetic tone is holding the rate down
The sinoatrial node is damaged
Both divisions are silent at rest
cards.explanation: A resting rate below the intrinsic rate can only mean an active brake, and vagal tone is that brake. Sympathetic tone pushes the rate up, so more of it would move the heart above 100 rather than below. A node that is damaged would not still be pacing normally, and if both divisions were silent the rate would sit at the intrinsic value.

cards.q: Both vagus nerves to the heart are blocked in a resting person while sympathetic fibers are left intact. Predict the heart rate.
cards.a: It rises above the previous resting rate.
options: It falls toward 40 beats per minute
It stays at the previous resting rate
It rises above the previous resting rate
It becomes irregular but averages the same
cards.explanation: Removing the dominant resting brake unmasks the intrinsic pacemaker rate plus whatever sympathetic tone remains, so the rate climbs. A fall would require losing sympathetic rather than vagal input. Staying the same would only happen if vagal tone had been absent, and while beat to beat variability does drop after vagal block, the average rate clearly increases.

cards.q: Sympathetic fibers to the heart are blocked in a resting person while vagal fibers stay intact. Predict the change in heart rate.
cards.a: It falls modestly, because sympathetic tone at rest is small.
options: It falls to about half the resting value
It rises toward the intrinsic rate
It is unchanged, since only exercise uses sympathetic fibers
It falls modestly, because sympathetic tone at rest is small
cards.explanation: At rest the sympathetic contribution to heart rate is the smaller of the two, so removing it lowers the rate somewhat but leaves the vagally braked pace largely intact. Halving the rate overstates a tone that is minor at rest. A rise would follow vagal block, not sympathetic block, and sympathetic fibers do fire at rest rather than only during exercise.

cards.q: Sympathetic firing to the arterioles of the skin decreases. Predict what happens to those vessels.
cards.a: They dilate, because the constricting tone is reduced.
options: They dilate, because the constricting tone is reduced
They constrict, because parasympathetic input takes over
They stay the same, since tone is fixed
They dilate, because parasympathetic fibers are activated
cards.explanation: The resting vessel is held partly closed by sympathetic tone, so a fall in firing releases that grip and the vessel widens, which is exactly how skin flow rises when the body needs to lose heat. No parasympathetic supply exists in these vessels, so both options invoking it are wrong regardless of the direction they predict. Tone is a variable firing rate, not a fixed setting.

cards.q: A drug blocks both autonomic divisions at the heart completely. Predict the resulting heart rate.
cards.a: About 100 beats per minute.
options: About 40 beats per minute
About 100 beats per minute
About 70 beats per minute
Zero, since the heart needs neural input
cards.explanation: With both inputs gone the sinoatrial node runs at its own intrinsic rate of roughly 100 beats per minute, so the rate rises rather than falls. About 70 is the rate with normal tone present, mostly vagal. About 40 would suggest a slower pacemaker taking over, and the heart does not stop, since the node depolarizes spontaneously without any nerve supply.

cards.q: Parasympathetic input to the small intestine is removed while sympathetic input remains. Predict the change in motility.
cards.a: Motility falls, because the stimulating input is gone and the inhibitory input is unopposed.
options: Motility rises, because the input that normally inhibits the gut has been removed
Motility is unchanged, since the enteric nervous system runs the gut on its own
Motility falls, because the stimulating input is gone and the inhibitory input is unopposed
Motility rises briefly and then stops entirely a few minutes later
cards.explanation: The parasympathetic division stimulates the gut, so removing it takes away the accelerator and leaves the sympathetic brake acting alone, which lowers motility. Calling the parasympathetic input inhibitory reverses the roles of the two divisions at this organ. The enteric system does keep some activity going, so motility falls rather than stopping, and there is no initial surge.

cards.q: Why does losing one division change a dually innervated organ less dramatically than losing the only division supplying a singly innervated organ?
cards.a: The remaining division still acts on the organ and can be adjusted up or down.
options: Singly innervated organs have no intrinsic or local activity of their own to fall back on
The remaining division still acts on the organ and can be adjusted up or down
Dually innervated organs regenerate their lost nerve supply much faster than other organs
Singly innervated organs are controlled by hormones rather than by nerves at all
cards.explanation: In a dually innervated organ the surviving division still delivers a graded, adjustable signal, so control is reduced rather than lost. Singly innervated targets such as arterioles do have intrinsic and local control, so an absence of intrinsic activity is not the reason. Nerve regeneration speed does not differ by innervation pattern, and hormones supplement rather than replace innervation.

cards.q: A resting subject with a heart rate of 72 is given a drug that blocks vagal input to the heart, and the rate rises to 96. A second subject is given a drug that blocks sympathetic input, and the rate falls from 72 to 64. What do these results show about resting autonomic tone at the heart?
cards.a: Parasympathetic tone is much greater than sympathetic tone at rest.
options: Sympathetic tone is much greater than parasympathetic tone at rest
Parasympathetic tone is much greater than sympathetic tone at rest
The two tones are equal, since both drugs changed the rate
Neither tone exists at rest, since the node sets its own rate
cards.explanation: The size of the change after each block measures the tone that was removed, and losing the vagus moved the rate by 24 beats while losing sympathetic input moved it by only 8, so the vagal brake was doing most of the work. Equal tones would produce equal shifts in opposite directions. Both tones clearly exist at rest, since blocking either one moved the rate away from 72.

cards.q: A person whose vagal supply to the heart has been interrupted begins moderate exercise. Predict the resting rate before exercise and the ability to raise rate during exercise.
cards.a: Resting rate is elevated, and rate can still rise because sympathetic fibers are intact.
options: Resting rate is elevated, and rate can still rise because sympathetic fibers are intact
Resting rate is normal, but the heart is unable to raise its rate at all during exercise
Resting rate is lower than usual, and the rate still rises normally during exercise
Resting rate is elevated, and the heart is already at its ceiling and cannot rise further
cards.explanation: Without vagal tone the baseline sits near the intrinsic rate, which is higher than normal, and because the sympathetic supply is untouched the usual exercise increase still occurs, although the total range from rest to peak is narrower. A normal or low resting rate would require vagal tone that is no longer present. The heart is not at its ceiling at rest, so further increase remains possible.

cards.q: All sympathetic fibers to one arm are cut. Predict the blood flow and skin temperature in that arm compared with the other arm shortly afterward.
cards.a: Flow is higher and the skin is warmer, because vasomotor tone was removed.
options: Flow is lower and the skin is cooler, because the vessels lost their nerve supply
Flow is higher and the skin is warmer, because vasomotor tone was removed
Flow and temperature are unchanged, since parasympathetic fibers take over
Flow is higher but the skin is cooler, because sweating increases
cards.explanation: Sympathetic fibers hold these vessels partly constricted, so cutting them removes the constricting tone, the arterioles widen, and warm blood flows more freely into the skin. Expecting cooling treats the sympathetic input as a dilator, which reverses its role in most vascular beds. There are no parasympathetic fibers to compensate, and sweating decreases rather than increases after sympathetic denervation, since sweat glands are sympathetic targets.

cards.q: Salivary glands are unusual in that both divisions increase secretion, the parasympathetic producing copious watery saliva and the sympathetic a small thick volume. Predict what happens to salivary output if parasympathetic input alone is removed.
cards.a: Output falls sharply and what remains is scant and thick.
options: Output rises, since the opposing division is now unopposed
Output is unchanged, since the sympathetic supply is equivalent
Output falls sharply and what remains is scant and thick
Output stops completely, since the gland has only one supply
cards.explanation: Here the two divisions cooperate rather than oppose, so losing the parasympathetic side removes the main source of watery secretion and leaves only the small thick sympathetic contribution. Expecting a rise applies the antagonistic model that does not hold at this gland. The two supplies are not equivalent in volume, and secretion does not stop because the sympathetic supply survives.

cards.q: The secretory cells of the adrenal medulla are best described as modified versions of which cell?
cards.a: Postganglionic sympathetic neurons.
options: Postganglionic sympathetic neurons
Preganglionic sympathetic neurons
Postganglionic parasympathetic neurons
Skeletal muscle fibers
cards.explanation: Chromaffin cells develop from the same neural crest tissue as postganglionic sympathetic neurons and sit in the same position in the pathway, one synapse downstream of the CNS. Preganglionic neurons are the cells that innervate them, not the cells themselves. There is no parasympathetic component to the medulla, and chromaffin cells are secretory rather than contractile.

cards.q: Which fibers innervate the cells of the adrenal medulla?
cards.a: Sympathetic preganglionic fibers.
options: Sympathetic postganglionic fibers
Sympathetic preganglionic fibers
Parasympathetic preganglionic fibers
Somatic motor fibers
cards.explanation: Preganglionic sympathetic axons run through the chain without synapsing and end directly on the chromaffin cells, which is exactly the arrangement seen at any sympathetic ganglion. Postganglionic fibers would imply a synapse had already happened somewhere else. The medulla receives no parasympathetic or somatic supply.

cards.q: Which transmitter and receptor are used where the nerve meets the adrenal medullary cells?
cards.a: Acetylcholine acting on nicotinic receptors.
options: Norepinephrine acting on beta-1 receptors
Acetylcholine acting on muscarinic receptors
Acetylcholine acting on nicotinic receptors
Epinephrine acting on alpha-1 receptors
cards.explanation: This synapse follows the ganglionic rule exactly, acetylcholine released by a preganglionic fiber onto nicotinic receptors, which is the strongest evidence that the medulla is a modified ganglion. Muscarinic receptors would place the synapse at a parasympathetic target instead. Norepinephrine and epinephrine act on adrenergic receptors at the far end of the pathway, not at the ganglionic step.

cards.q: Which catecholamine makes up the majority of adrenal medullary secretion?
cards.a: Epinephrine.
options: Norepinephrine
Dopamine
Acetylcholine
Epinephrine
cards.explanation: About eighty percent of the output is epinephrine and most of the rest is norepinephrine, so the medulla is the body main source of circulating epinephrine. Norepinephrine is the minority product here even though it is the transmitter at ordinary sympathetic nerve endings. Dopamine is released in trace amounts, and acetylcholine is the input to these cells rather than their product.

cards.q: Where does the adrenal medulla release its secretions?
cards.a: Into the bloodstream.
options: Into the bloodstream
Into a synaptic cleft at the target organ
Into the interstitial fluid of the kidney only
Into the lumen of a duct
cards.explanation: Chromaffin cells secrete into capillaries, so their catecholamines act as hormones and reach every tissue with the appropriate receptors. Release into a synaptic cleft is what an ordinary postganglionic neuron does, and it is the difference that makes the medullary response broader and longer. The medulla is not a duct gland and its secretion is not confined to the kidney, despite the location of the adrenal glands.

cards.q: What structural feature do adrenal medullary cells lack that ordinary postganglionic sympathetic neurons have?
cards.a: An axon.
options: A cell body
An axon
Nicotinic receptors
Secretory vesicles
cards.explanation: Chromaffin cells kept the secretory machinery of a sympathetic neuron but never grew an axon, so instead of delivering transmitter to one target they dump it into the blood. They certainly have cell bodies, and they carry nicotinic receptors just as any postganglionic neuron does. They are full of secretory vesicles, which is how the catecholamines are stored before release.

cards.q: How long do the effects of circulating catecholamines from the adrenal medulla last compared with the effects of direct sympathetic nerve stimulation?
cards.a: Considerably longer, lasting seconds to minutes after the stimulus ends.
options: Considerably shorter, ending within a few milliseconds of the stimulus
Exactly the same, since the transmitter molecules involved are identical
Considerably longer, lasting seconds to minutes after the stimulus ends
Longer only in those tissues that also receive direct sympathetic innervation
cards.explanation: Hormonal catecholamines linger in the blood for a period measured in minutes, so the response outlasts the nerve traffic that triggered it, while a nerve released transmitter is cleared from the cleft almost at once. Identical transmitters do not mean identical time courses, because how the molecule is removed differs completely. The prolonged effect appears in every responsive tissue, innervated or not.

cards.q: Why is norepinephrine removed from a sympathetic synapse so much faster than circulating epinephrine is removed from the blood?
cards.a: The nerve terminal takes it back up almost immediately.
options: It is destroyed by acetylcholinesterase in the cleft
It diffuses into bone and is stored there
It is filtered by the kidney within milliseconds
The nerve terminal takes it back up almost immediately
cards.explanation: Reuptake into the presynaptic terminal clears the cleft within a fraction of a second, while a hormone in the blood must wait for enzymes in the liver and other tissues to break it down. Acetylcholinesterase acts on acetylcholine and has no effect on catecholamines. Bone storage is not a route of removal, and renal handling takes far longer than milliseconds.

cards.q: A gland is found in which a preganglionic fiber ends directly on secretory cells that carry nicotinic receptors and release catecholamines. How should this gland be classified?
cards.a: As a modified sympathetic ganglion.
options: As a modified sympathetic ganglion
As a terminal ganglion of the parasympathetic division
As an ordinary endocrine gland with no neural connection at all
As an effector organ of the somatic motor system
cards.explanation: The pattern of a preganglionic fiber, a nicotinic synapse, and cells that release catecholamines is the sympathetic ganglion pattern, with the single change that the output goes into the blood instead of down an axon. A parasympathetic terminal ganglion would release acetylcholine onto muscarinic receptors nearby. An ordinary endocrine gland is controlled hormonally rather than by a preganglionic nerve, and a somatic effector would be skeletal muscle.

cards.q: A drug blocks nicotinic receptors throughout the body. Predict its effect on adrenal medullary secretion.
cards.a: Secretion falls, because the synapse onto chromaffin cells is nicotinic.
options: Secretion rises, since the inhibitory input is removed
Secretion falls, because the synapse onto chromaffin cells is nicotinic
Secretion is unchanged, since the medulla is hormonally controlled
Secretion is unchanged, since chromaffin cells use muscarinic receptors
cards.explanation: The only drive to the chromaffin cells arrives through a nicotinic synapse, so blocking that receptor silences the gland. The input is excitatory rather than inhibitory, so removing it cannot raise output. The medulla is not under hormonal control from the pituitary the way the adrenal cortex is, and its receptors are nicotinic, not muscarinic.

cards.q: A stimulus activates both the sympathetic nerves to the heart and the adrenal medulla, then stops. Which influence on the heart fades first?
cards.a: The direct nerve effect, because transmitter is cleared from the synapse rapidly.
options: The hormonal effect, because the hormone is quickly diluted in the circulating blood
Both fade together, since the two act on the same cardiac receptors
The direct nerve effect, because transmitter is cleared from the synapse rapidly
Neither fades, since the effects of catecholamines are permanent
cards.explanation: Reuptake ends the synaptic signal in under a second, while circulating catecholamines keep acting for minutes until they are metabolized, so the nerve effect disappears first. Dilution does lower hormone concentration but does not clear it faster than reuptake clears a cleft. Acting on the same beta-1 receptors does not equalize the two time courses, since duration is set by removal, and no catecholamine effect is permanent.

cards.q: The adrenal medulla is removed while all sympathetic nerves are left intact. Predict the response to a sudden fright.
cards.a: A sympathetic response still occurs but is smaller and shorter lived.
options: No sympathetic response occurs anywhere in the body
The response is normal in size but takes much longer to begin
A sympathetic response still occurs but is smaller and shorter lived
The response is larger than normal, since a hormonal brake has been removed
cards.explanation: Direct innervation still reaches the heart, vessels, and other targets, so the immediate response happens, but without the circulating catecholamines it is less widespread and fades as soon as nerve traffic stops. A complete absence of response would require losing the sympathetic nerves themselves. Onset actually depends on the nerves, which are the faster route, and the medullary output is excitatory, so its loss cannot enlarge the response.

cards.q: Circulating epinephrine reaches a bronchiole that receives little or no direct sympathetic innervation. Predict the effect on that airway.
cards.a: It dilates, because beta-2 receptors are reached through the blood.
options: It dilates, because beta-2 receptors are reached through the blood
It is unaffected, because a hormone cannot act on a tissue that lacks innervation
It constricts, because epinephrine acts on alpha-1 receptors in the airway wall
It is unaffected, because epinephrine is unable to leave the capillary bed
cards.explanation: A hormone only needs a receptor, not a nerve ending, so beta-2 receptors on airway smooth muscle respond to blood borne epinephrine and the bronchiole widens. Requiring innervation confuses a hormonal signal with a synaptic one. Alpha-1 receptors dominate on most vascular smooth muscle rather than on airways, and catecholamines cross capillary walls readily.

cards.q: Which route delivers its effect to the heart sooner after the central nervous system commands a sympathetic response?
cards.a: The direct sympathetic nerve, since it does not depend on circulation time.
options: The adrenal medulla, since its hormones reach a larger number of receptors
The direct sympathetic nerve, since it does not depend on circulation time
Both arrive at the same instant, since a single central command triggers both routes
The adrenal medulla, since epinephrine binds the beta-1 receptor more tightly
cards.explanation: The nerve delivers transmitter directly onto the node in milliseconds, while the hormone must be secreted, enter the blood, and be carried to the heart, which takes several seconds. Acting on more receptors changes how widespread the effect is, not how quickly it starts. A single central command does trigger both routes, but they arrive on very different timescales, and receptor affinity does not shorten circulation time.

cards.q: A person is startled, and the fright passes in a second, yet the heart is still racing two minutes later. Trace the reason.
cards.a: Catecholamines released into the blood from the adrenal medulla are still circulating and acting on cardiac beta-1 receptors.
options: Sympathetic nerves to the heart continue firing at a high rate for minutes after the startling stimulus ends
Catecholamines released into the blood from the adrenal medulla are still circulating and acting on cardiac beta-1 receptors
Acetylcholine accumulated at the sinoatrial node during the startle and keeps those pacemaker cells depolarized
The vagus nerve was inactivated by the startle and needs several minutes to recover its resting activity
cards.explanation: The same preganglionic burst that drove the cardiac nerves also drove the chromaffin cells, and hormonal catecholamines are cleared over minutes rather than milliseconds, so the beta-1 effect on the node outlasts the nerve traffic. Nerve firing tracks the stimulus and stops with it. Acetylcholine slows the node rather than speeding it, and the vagus is not switched off for minutes by a single startle.

cards.q: In an experiment, brief stimulation of the cardiac sympathetic nerve and brief stimulation of the nerve to the adrenal medulla are compared. How do the two heart rate responses differ in onset and in duration?
cards.a: The nerve response starts sooner and ends sooner, while the medullary response starts later and lasts longer.
options: The nerve response starts later than the medullary response and also lasts considerably longer than it does
Both responses start and end at the same time, since both of them act on the same cardiac beta-1 receptors
The nerve response starts sooner and ends sooner, while the medullary response starts later and lasts longer
The medullary response starts sooner, because hormones are carried in fast moving arterial blood
cards.explanation: Direct innervation wins on speed because there is no transport step, and hormonal release wins on duration because clearance from blood is slow compared with synaptic reuptake, so the two routes trade off against each other. Reversing the pattern ignores both the circulation delay and the difference in clearance. Sharing a receptor does not equalize the timing, since timing depends on delivery and removal rather than on the receptor.

cards.q: A ganglionic blocking agent prevents transmission at nicotinic receptors in all autonomic ganglia. Predict its effect on direct sympathetic output to blood vessels and on adrenal catecholamine release.
cards.a: Both are lost, because both depend on the same nicotinic synapse.
options: Both are lost, because both depend on the same nicotinic synapse
Direct output is lost but medullary release continues
Direct output continues but medullary release is lost
Neither is affected, since sympathetic targets use adrenergic receptors
cards.explanation: The chromaffin cell synapse is a ganglionic synapse in everything but name, so an agent that blocks nicotinic transmission silences the medulla at the same time it silences ordinary sympathetic ganglia, and both branches of sympathetic output fail together. Sparing either one treats the medulla as if it sat outside the sympathetic pathway. The adrenergic receptors on the targets are downstream and are never reached, because nothing gets past the blocked relay.

cards.q: During prolonged exercise, blood epinephrine rises and remains elevated while a subject sustains a high heart rate. If the same subject had only direct sympathetic innervation and no adrenal medulla, what would change about the cardiovascular response?
cards.a: The response would still begin promptly but would depend entirely on ongoing nerve traffic and would reach fewer poorly innervated tissues.
options: The response would begin noticeably later than normal but would still climb to the same peak
The response would still begin promptly but would depend entirely on ongoing nerve traffic and would reach fewer poorly innervated tissues
The heart rate could not rise at all, because a sustained rise depends on circulating epinephrine rather than on nerves
The response would be identical in size and in duration, since the nerve and the hormone do the same job
cards.explanation: Nerves supply the fast, targeted component and the medulla supplies a slower, broader, longer lasting component, so removing the hormone leaves onset intact but makes the response narrower in reach and immediately reversible when firing stops. Onset would not be delayed, since the nerves are the faster route. The heart is directly innervated and its rate would still rise, and the two routes are complementary rather than identical.

cards.q: A beta blocker occupies which receptor?
cards.a: The beta adrenergic receptor.
options: The beta adrenergic receptor
The muscarinic cholinergic receptor
The nicotinic cholinergic receptor
The alpha adrenergic receptor
cards.explanation: A beta blocker sits on beta adrenergic receptors, the sites where norepinephrine and epinephrine normally act on the heart and on certain smooth muscle. Muscarinic and nicotinic receptors bind acetylcholine and belong to a different transmitter system entirely. Alpha receptors are adrenergic but are a separate subtype, dominant on most vascular smooth muscle rather than on the heart.

cards.q: What does a receptor antagonist do at the receptor it occupies?
cards.a: It binds without activating and prevents the normal ligand from acting.
options: It activates the receptor even more strongly than the natural ligand does
It binds without activating and prevents the normal ligand from acting
It destroys the receptor protein permanently and irreversibly
It increases the amount of transmitter that is released onto the receptor
cards.explanation: An antagonist occupies the binding site but produces no signal, so the natural transmitter can no longer reach the receptor and its usual effect on the organ is lost. Producing a stronger effect describes an agonist. Antagonists do not destroy receptors, and they act on the receiving side rather than changing how much transmitter is released.

cards.q: A muscarinic antagonist prevents which transmitter from acting at parasympathetic target organs?
cards.a: Acetylcholine.
options: Norepinephrine
Epinephrine
Acetylcholine
Dopamine
cards.explanation: Muscarinic receptors are the acetylcholine receptors on parasympathetic targets, so blocking them removes the effect of acetylcholine released by postganglionic parasympathetic fibers. Norepinephrine and epinephrine act on alpha and beta receptors and are unaffected by this block. Dopamine is not the transmitter at autonomic effector organs.

cards.q: Does a muscarinic antagonist interfere with transmission at the skeletal neuromuscular junction?
cards.a: No, because that junction uses nicotinic receptors.
options: Yes, because both of these sites use acetylcholine
Yes, but only at high doses and only in cardiac muscle
No, because the neuromuscular junction uses norepinephrine instead
No, because that junction uses nicotinic receptors
cards.explanation: Sharing a transmitter is not the same as sharing a receptor, and the neuromuscular junction carries nicotinic receptors that a muscarinic blocker does not fit. Answering yes because both sites use acetylcholine makes exactly the mistake this card is designed to catch.
