The neuromuscular junction does not use norepinephrine, and cardiac muscle is not a skeletal neuromuscular junction.

cards.q: Which receptor subtype on the heart is the main target of a beta-1 selective blocker?
cards.a: Beta-1.
options: Beta-2
Muscarinic
Alpha-1
Beta-1
cards.explanation: Beta-1 receptors dominate on cardiac tissue, so a blocker selective for that subtype has its main effect on the heart. Beta-2 receptors are found on bronchiolar smooth muscle and on skeletal muscle vessels, which is why a selective agent leaves airways relatively alone. Alpha-1 receptors are on most vascular smooth muscle, and muscarinic receptors on the heart are cholinergic and unaffected by a beta blocker.

cards.q: Which division's influence on the heart is reduced by a beta blocker?
cards.a: The sympathetic division.
options: The parasympathetic division
Both divisions equally
The sympathetic division
Neither, since the heart is not innervated
cards.explanation: Beta-1 receptors are the sympathetic receptors on the heart, so blocking them removes sympathetic influence and leaves vagal influence intact and relatively unopposed. The parasympathetic effect on the heart runs through muscarinic receptors and would need a different blocker. The heart is dually innervated, so both statements denying innervation or claiming equal effect are wrong.

cards.q: Which division's influence on the gut is reduced by a muscarinic antagonist?
cards.a: The parasympathetic division.
options: The sympathetic division
The somatic motor system
Both divisions equally
The parasympathetic division
cards.explanation: The gut receives parasympathetic acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors, so blocking those receptors removes the main stimulating input to intestinal smooth muscle. Sympathetic influence on the gut works through adrenergic receptors and is left in place. The gut has no somatic motor supply to its smooth muscle, so no somatic effect is possible.

cards.q: A nonselective beta blocker acts at which receptors?
cards.a: Both beta-1 and beta-2 receptors.
options: Both beta-1 and beta-2 receptors
Beta-1 receptors on the heart and alpha-1 receptors on vessels
Beta-2 receptors and muscarinic receptors together
Beta-1 receptors on the heart only
cards.explanation: Nonselective means the agent does not distinguish between the beta subtypes, so it occupies beta-1 receptors on the heart and beta-2 receptors on airway and skeletal muscle vessels alike. Adding alpha-1 or muscarinic receptors to the list crosses into different receptor families that a beta blocker does not fit. Beta-1 only would describe a selective agent instead.

cards.q: A beta blocker reaches the heart of a resting person. Predict the effect on heart rate.
cards.a: Heart rate falls.
options: Heart rate rises
Heart rate becomes irregular but averages the same
Heart rate is unchanged
Heart rate falls
cards.explanation: Blocking beta-1 receptors removes the sympathetic push on the sinoatrial node, so the node depolarizes more slowly and the rate drops toward or below the value set by vagal tone alone. A rise would follow removal of the vagal brake, which a beta blocker does not touch. Some sympathetic tone is present even at rest, so the rate does change.

cards.q: A muscarinic antagonist reaches the heart of a resting person. Predict the effect on heart rate.
cards.a: Heart rate rises.
options: Heart rate falls
Heart rate is unchanged
Heart rate rises
Heart rate falls, then returns to baseline
cards.explanation: Muscarinic receptors carry the vagal signal to the sinoatrial node, so blocking them removes the resting brake and the rate climbs toward the intrinsic pacemaker rate. A fall would follow blockade of beta-1 receptors instead. Because vagal tone dominates the resting heart, this change is substantial rather than absent.

cards.q: A muscarinic antagonist reaches the small intestine. Predict the effect on motility.
cards.a: Motility decreases.
options: Motility increases
Motility increases then stops abruptly
Motility is unchanged
Motility decreases
cards.explanation: Parasympathetic acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors is the main stimulus to intestinal smooth muscle, so blocking those receptors slows the gut. An increase would require blocking the sympathetic input instead, which is the inhibitory one here. Enteric activity persists, so motility is reduced rather than abolished, but it is clearly changed.

cards.q: A nonselective beta blocker reaches the bronchioles. Predict the effect on airway diameter.
cards.a: The airways narrow somewhat, because beta-2 mediated relaxation is lost.
options: The airways widen, because beta-2 receptors normally constrict them
The airways widen, because this blocker occupies muscarinic receptors as well
The airways are unaffected, since airway smooth muscle carries only muscarinic receptors
The airways narrow somewhat, because beta-2 mediated relaxation is lost
cards.explanation: Beta-2 receptors normally relax airway smooth muscle in response to circulating epinephrine, so blocking them removes a dilating influence and leaves the airway narrower than it would otherwise be. Calling beta-2 a constrictor reverses its action. Airways carry both muscarinic and beta-2 receptors, and a beta blocker has no effect at muscarinic sites.

cards.q: A muscarinic antagonist reaches the salivary glands. Predict the effect on saliva production.
cards.a: It falls markedly, producing a dry mouth.
options: It rises, because sympathetic secretion is now completely unopposed
It is unchanged, since the salivary glands receive sympathetic fibers only
It falls markedly, producing a dry mouth
It rises, because blocking a receptor increases secretion from the gland
cards.explanation: Watery salivary secretion is driven by parasympathetic acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors, so removing that signal leaves only the small thick sympathetic contribution and the mouth feels dry. The sympathetic supply cannot compensate in volume. Salivary glands do receive parasympathetic fibers, and blocking a receptor removes an effect rather than creating one.

cards.q: A beta blocker reaches the ventricular myocardium. Predict the effect on the force of contraction.
cards.a: Force decreases.
options: Force increases
Force is unchanged, since beta receptors affect heart rate only
Force decreases
Force increases at rest but decreases once exercise begins
cards.explanation: Beta-1 receptors on working myocardium increase calcium entry and therefore contractile force, so blocking them lowers the force of each beat as well as the rate. Restricting beta effects to rate alone misses the contractility half of the cardiac response. Blocking an excitatory receptor cannot raise force under any condition.

cards.q: A person takes a nonselective beta blocker. Predict the combined effect on the heart and on the bronchioles.
cards.a: The heart slows and contracts less forcefully, and the bronchioles narrow.
options: The heart slows and contracts less forcefully, and the bronchioles narrow
The heart slows and contracts less forcefully, while the bronchioles widen at the same time
The heart speeds up, while the bronchioles narrow at the same time
The heart is left unaffected, and only the bronchioles narrow in response
cards.explanation: The same agent hits beta-1 receptors on the heart, lowering rate and force, and beta-2 receptors on airway smooth muscle, removing the relaxing influence so the airways narrow, which is why airway effects matter with nonselective agents. Widening airways would require the beta-2 receptor to be constrictor, which it is not. A faster heart would follow muscarinic blockade instead, and the heart cannot be spared by an agent that occupies beta-1 receptors.

cards.q: A person receives a muscarinic antagonist. Predict the effect on heart rate and on gastrointestinal motility.
cards.a: Heart rate rises and gastrointestinal motility falls.
options: Heart rate falls and gastrointestinal motility rises
Both heart rate and gastrointestinal motility fall
Heart rate rises and gastrointestinal motility falls
Both heart rate and gastrointestinal motility rise
cards.explanation: Removing parasympathetic influence produces opposite changes in the two organs, because that division normally slows the heart and speeds the gut, so blocking it releases the heart and quiets the gut. Falling rate with rising motility describes adding parasympathetic activity rather than blocking it. The two options that move both in the same direction miss the fact that the same division has opposite effects on these targets.

cards.q: A person taking a beta-1 selective blocker begins moderate exercise. Predict the heart rate response compared with the same exercise without the drug.
cards.a: Heart rate still rises but reaches a lower peak.
options: Heart rate is unable to rise at all during the exercise
Heart rate falls even further as the exercise continues
Heart rate rises to the same peak value but does so more slowly
Heart rate still rises but reaches a lower peak
cards.explanation: Blockade is competitive and partial, and withdrawal of vagal tone still contributes to the early rise, so the rate increases but the sympathetic beta-1 contribution is blunted and the ceiling is lower. Complete inability to rise overstates the block and ignores vagal withdrawal. The peak is reduced rather than merely delayed, and a further fall during exercise contradicts the normal direction of the exercise response.

cards.q: After a drug is given, a subject shows a faster heart rate, reduced gastric secretion, and slowed intestinal motility, while arteriolar resistance is unchanged. Which receptor was blocked?
cards.a: The muscarinic receptor.
options: The beta-1 receptor
The alpha-1 receptor
The muscarinic receptor
The nicotinic receptor
cards.explanation: Every finding points to loss of parasympathetic effect at target organs, and unchanged arteriolar resistance fits because most vessels have no parasympathetic supply, so a muscarinic block leaves them alone. Blocking beta-1 receptors would have slowed the heart rather than speeding it. Blocking alpha-1 receptors would have lowered arteriolar resistance, and blocking nicotinic receptors would have shut down both divisions and dropped vascular resistance as well.

cards.q: What does heart rate variability measure?
cards.a: The beat to beat variation in the interval between successive heartbeats.
options: The beat to beat variation in the interval between successive heartbeats
The difference between the highest and the lowest heart rate reached during exercise
The variation in the size of the R wave recorded from one beat to the next
The change in heart rate measured between sitting and standing
cards.explanation: Heart rate variability is calculated from the intervals between successive R waves, so it describes how much the timing of the heartbeat fluctuates from one beat to the next. The exercise range and the sitting to standing change are separate measures of cardiovascular reserve and of the orthostatic response. Variation in R wave amplitude reflects electrode position and body movement rather than autonomic control.

cards.q: Which autonomic division is chiefly responsible for the rapid beat to beat component of heart rate variability?
cards.a: The parasympathetic division.
options: The sympathetic division
Neither, since variability comes from the sinoatrial node alone
Both contribute equally to fast changes
The parasympathetic division
cards.explanation: Vagal effects on the sinoatrial node begin and end within a single beat, so only the parasympathetic division can make heart rate fluctuate that quickly. Sympathetic effects work through a slower second messenger pathway and take seconds to build and decay, so they shape slower trends rather than beat to beat swings. The node alone would produce a very regular rhythm, which is why a denervated heart shows little variability.

cards.q: In respiratory sinus arrhythmia, what happens to heart rate during inspiration?
cards.a: It increases.
options: It decreases
It stays constant
It becomes irregular without a consistent direction
It increases
cards.explanation: Vagal traffic to the heart falls during inspiration, so the brake is briefly lifted and the rate rises, then falls again on expiration as vagal activity returns. A slowing during inspiration reverses the pattern. A constant rate would mean the vagal modulation is absent, which is itself a finding in people with reduced parasympathetic control, and the pattern is consistent enough to be timed against the breathing cycle.

cards.q: How is a cold pressor test performed?
cards.a: The hand is immersed in ice water for one to two minutes while blood pressure is recorded.
options: The subject breathes chilled air for several minutes while heart rate is recorded continuously
The whole body is cooled with a fan until the subject begins to shiver visibly
Ice is applied to the skin of the neck over the carotid sinus for a full minute
The hand is immersed in ice water for one to two minutes while blood pressure is recorded
cards.explanation: Immersing a hand in ice water delivers a strong painful cold stimulus, and blood pressure is measured during the immersion to gauge the sympathetic response. Cooling the whole body or breathing cold air produces slower thermoregulatory changes rather than the sharp pressor response being tested. Pressure on the carotid sinus is a different maneuver that tests the baroreceptor reflex.

cards.q: What is the expected blood pressure response during a cold pressor test?
cards.a: Blood pressure rises.
options: Blood pressure falls
Blood pressure is unchanged
Blood pressure falls then rises above baseline
Blood pressure rises
cards.explanation: The painful cold stimulus drives a sympathetic discharge that constricts arterioles and raises peripheral resistance, so systolic and diastolic pressure both climb within a minute. A fall would indicate the sympathetic response is not occurring. There is no initial drop, since the reflex is a direct pressor response rather than a baroreceptor mediated one.

cards.q: What does an orthostatic challenge consist of?
cards.a: Moving from lying down to standing while heart rate and blood pressure are recorded.
options: Moving from lying down to standing while heart rate and blood pressure are recorded
Holding a forced expiration against a closed airway for fifteen seconds
Exercising on a stationary cycle at a fixed workload for several minutes
Breathing deeply and slowly at a paced six breaths per minute
cards.explanation: The orthostatic test uses the change in posture itself as the stimulus, since standing shifts blood into the legs and challenges the reflexes that defend blood pressure. Forced expiration against a closed airway is the Valsalva maneuver, and paced deep breathing is used to test respiratory sinus arrhythmia. Fixed workload exercise measures cardiovascular fitness rather than the postural reflex.

cards.q: Which recording is used to obtain the intervals from which heart rate variability is calculated?
cards.a: The electrocardiogram, using the time between successive R waves.
options: The electrocardiogram, using the time between successive R waves
A spirometer trace, using the time between successive breaths
A blood pressure cuff, using the systolic value from each beat
A pulse oximeter, using the oxygen saturation value from each beat
cards.explanation: The R wave is sharp and easy to time precisely, so the R to R interval on the electrocardiogram is the standard measurement for variability. A spirometer records breathing, which is a driver of variability but not the measurement itself. Cuff pressures and oxygen saturation do not resolve individual beats with the precision needed.

cards.q: What blood pressure change within three minutes of standing defines orthostatic hypotension?
cards.a: A fall of at least 20 mmHg systolic or at least 10 mmHg diastolic.
options: A fall of at least 5 mmHg systolic or at least 5 mmHg diastolic
A rise of at least 20 mmHg in the systolic pressure
Any measurable fall in the mean arterial pressure at all
A fall of at least 20 mmHg systolic or at least 10 mmHg diastolic
cards.explanation: The accepted threshold is a drop of 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic within three minutes of standing, large enough to exceed the small transient dip that healthy people show. A 5 mmHg change is within the normal transient response and would label almost everyone. A rise describes the opposite finding, and any fall at all is too loose a criterion to be useful.

cards.q: A resting subject shows large beat to beat variation in R to R interval. How should this be interpreted?
cards.a: As parasympathetic dominance at the heart.
options: As parasympathetic dominance at the heart
As sympathetic dominance at the heart
As loss of all autonomic input to the heart
As a faulty electrode connection
cards.explanation: High variability at rest reflects strong, rapidly changing vagal influence on the sinoatrial node, which is the hallmark of parasympathetic dominance. Sympathetic dominance produces a faster and more regular rhythm because its effects change slowly. A heart stripped of autonomic input beats with very little variability, which is the opposite finding, and a genuine variability pattern tracks the breathing cycle rather than appearing as random noise.

cards.q: During a cold pressor test, blood pressure rises. Which mechanism accounts for most of the rise?
cards.a: Alpha-1 mediated arteriolar constriction raising peripheral resistance.
options: Alpha-1 mediated arteriolar constriction raising peripheral resistance
Beta-2 mediated dilation of the vessels supplying skeletal muscle
Withdrawal of resting vagal tone from the arterioles
Increased compliance of the veins in the legs
cards.explanation: Sympathetic outflow triggered by the painful stimulus reaches alpha-1 receptors on arterioles throughout the body, and the resulting rise in total peripheral resistance is the main driver of the pressure increase. Beta-2 dilation lowers resistance and would work against the response. Arterioles have essentially no vagal supply, so there is no vagal tone there to withdraw, and greater venous compliance would reduce venous return rather than raise pressure.

cards.q: A subject stands up from lying down and heart rate rises by 15 beats per minute within 15 seconds. How is this interpreted?
cards.a: As a normal sympathetic response with vagal withdrawal.
options: As an abnormal parasympathetic surge
As a complete failure of the baroreceptor reflex
As clear evidence of orthostatic hypotension
As a normal sympathetic response with vagal withdrawal
cards.explanation: Standing unloads the baroreceptors, and the reflex answer is less vagal traffic and more sympathetic traffic to the heart, so a prompt rise of this size is the expected healthy result. A parasympathetic surge would slow the heart. Orthostatic hypotension is defined by a fall in blood pressure rather than by a rise in rate, and a working reflex is exactly what this response demonstrates.

cards.q: An electrocardiogram shows a steady R to R interval of 800 ms. What is the heart rate?
cards.a: 75 beats per minute.
options: 60 beats per minute
80 beats per minute
48 beats per minute
75 beats per minute
cards.explanation: There are 60000 ms in a minute, so dividing 60000 by an 800 ms interval gives 75 beats per minute. Choosing 80 comes from dividing 800 into a rounded number of seconds incorrectly, and 60 would be the rate if the interval were a full 1000 ms. A rate of 48 corresponds to an interval of about 1250 ms, much longer than the one recorded.

cards.q: A subject is asked to breathe slowly and deeply, and the record shows heart rate falling during each expiration. What causes the slowing?
cards.a: An increase in vagal activity to the sinoatrial node.
options: An increase in vagal activity to the sinoatrial node
An increase in the sympathetic activity reaching the ventricles
A decrease in the vagal activity reaching the sinoatrial node
A fall in arterial pressure that briefly unloads the baroreceptors
cards.explanation: Vagal traffic to the node rises during expiration and falls during inspiration, so the expiratory phase is when the brake is applied most strongly and the rate drops. Reduced vagal activity is what produces the inspiratory speeding, the other half of the same cycle. Sympathetic effects are too slow to shape single breaths, and unloading the baroreceptors would raise the rate rather than lower it.

cards.q: A resting subject shows a fast heart rate with almost no beat to beat variation. How should this be interpreted?
cards.a: As sympathetic dominance with reduced vagal influence.
options: As parasympathetic dominance with strong vagal influence
As an entirely normal finding during quiet breathing
As the sign of an unusually fit cardiovascular system
As sympathetic dominance with reduced vagal influence
cards.explanation: Losing the fast fluctuations means losing the vagal modulation that creates them, and a fast baseline rate points the same way, toward sympathetic dominance. Strong vagal influence produces the opposite pattern, a slower rate with wide variation. Trained endurance athletes typically show high variability with a low resting rate, and quiet breathing normally produces visible respiratory variation rather than none.

cards.q: A subject stands up. Trace the sequence from the mechanical effect of standing to the change in heart rate.
cards.a: Blood pools in the legs, venous return and stroke volume fall, baroreceptor firing drops, and sympathetic outflow rises to speed the heart.
options: Blood pools in the legs, venous return and stroke volume fall, baroreceptor firing drops, and sympathetic outflow rises to speed the heart
Blood shifts into the chest, stroke volume rises, baroreceptor firing rises, and vagal outflow then speeds the heart up
Blood pools in the legs, stroke volume falls, baroreceptor firing rises, and vagal outflow then slows the heart further
Blood pools in the legs, arterial pressure rises directly as a result, and the heart then slows down to compensate
cards.explanation: Gravity moves blood into the leg veins, so less returns to the heart, stroke volume falls, arterial pressure dips, the baroreceptors fire less, and the reflex answer is more sympathetic and less vagal drive, which raises the rate. The option that has blood shifting to the chest describes lying down rather than standing. The two options with rising baroreceptor firing get the direction backward, since a falling pressure means less stretch and less firing.

cards.q: On standing, a subject blood pressure falls 30 mmHg systolic and stays low, while heart rate rises by only 3 beats per minute. What does this pattern suggest?
cards.a: An inadequate sympathetic response to the orthostatic challenge.
options: An exaggerated sympathetic response to the orthostatic challenge
A normal response that requires no explanation
Excessive vagal withdrawal on standing
An inadequate sympathetic response to the orthostatic challenge
cards.explanation: A pressure drop of that size should trigger a brisk rise in heart rate and vasoconstriction, so the missing tachycardia points to a sympathetic limb that is not responding as it should. An exaggerated sympathetic response would show a large rise in rate and a defended pressure. Excessive vagal withdrawal would also speed the heart, again the opposite of what was recorded, and a sustained 30 mmHg fall meets the definition of orthostatic hypotension rather than a normal response.

cards.q: Two subjects are compared at rest. Subject A has a heart rate of 52 with wide beat to beat variation, and subject B has a heart rate of 88 with narrow variation. What is the most reasonable interpretation?
cards.a: Subject A is parasympathetically dominant and subject B is sympathetically dominant.
options: Subject A is parasympathetically dominant and subject B is sympathetically dominant
Subject A is sympathetically dominant and subject B is parasympathetically dominant
Both subjects are parasympathetically dominant, since both are at rest
Neither interpretation is possible without a cold pressor test
cards.explanation: A low rate with wide variability means strong vagal influence on the node, while a high rate with little variability means that vagal influence is reduced and sympathetic influence is relatively greater, so the two records sit at opposite ends of the same scale. Reversing the two assignments contradicts both the rate and the variability. Being at rest does not guarantee vagal dominance, and the resting record itself carries enough information to interpret, although a challenge test would add more.

cards.q: During a cold pressor test on a subject whose cardiac beta-1 receptors are blocked, blood pressure still rises substantially while heart rate barely changes. What explains the result?
cards.a: The pressure rise comes mainly from alpha-1 vasoconstriction, which the block does not affect.
options: The pressure rise came from a much larger stroke volume driven by cardiac beta-1 receptors
The pressure rise comes from a large increase in vagal tone to the arterioles
The block prevented the sympathetic discharge from occurring anywhere at all
The pressure rise comes mainly from alpha-1 vasoconstriction, which the block does not affect
cards.explanation: The cold pressor response raises pressure chiefly by narrowing arterioles through alpha-1 receptors, and those receptors are untouched by a beta-1 block, so resistance still climbs while the cardiac contribution is blunted and the rate stays flat. Arterioles have essentially no vagal supply, so increased vagal tone cannot be the source. A receptor block acts on the target rather than on the outflow itself, and a beta-1 driven stroke volume increase is precisely what the block prevented.
